title: Warnings to Judah's Last Kings
overview: Jeremiah confronts a line of Judah's kings, telling them their throne depends on justice for the vulnerable and announcing the downfall of each one in turn.

parts.label: A warning at the palace (vv. 1-9)
parts.note: Jeremiah tells the king that David's family will keep ruling only if it protects robbery victims, foreigners, orphans and widows and stops killing the innocent. Otherwise the palace, precious to God as the green hills of Gilead and built from Lebanon's cedar, will be cut down and burned, and passersby will say it fell because the people abandoned their covenant (binding agreement) with God.

parts.label: Weep for the exile (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: The dead king is Josiah, a good king killed in battle, and the people still mourned him. His son Shallum, also called Jehoahaz, ruled only three months before Egypt's king carried him off, so Jeremiah says to grieve for him instead, because he would die abroad and never come home.

parts.label: A palace built on unpaid work (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: This is aimed at Jehoiakim, another son of Josiah, who forced his own people to build him a lavish palace of cedar and red paint without paying them. Jeremiah contrasts him with Josiah, who lived well enough and stood up for the poor, and says that kind of justice is what it actually means to know God.

parts.label: No one will mourn him (vv. 18-19)
parts.note: Nobody will cry the usual funeral laments over Jehoiakim; he will be dragged off and dumped outside the city like a dead donkey, left unburied. The historical books do not clearly record how he died or was buried, so how this was fulfilled is uncertain.

parts.label: Jerusalem cries from the heights (vv. 20-23)
parts.note: Jerusalem is pictured as a woman shouting from the mountains of Lebanon, Bashan and Abarim because her allies, probably Egypt, have been crushed, and the wind will drive away her shepherds, meaning her leaders. Calling the city "Lebanon" pokes at its comfortable cedar palaces, which will not spare it pain as sharp as childbirth.

parts.label: The signet ring pulled off (vv. 24-30)
parts.note: A signet ring was a ring a ruler wore and used to stamp his seal on documents, yet God says that even if Jehoiachin (also called Coniah) were that ring on God's own hand, he would be pulled off and handed to Babylon, and he and his mother would die in exile. He did have children, but "record him as childless" means none of them would ever rule from David's throne.

think: Is it fair to judge a leader mainly by how the most vulnerable people under them are treated, rather than by what they build or achieve?
